newsitem.title: USA: Supreme Court reverses lower court in property case.
newsitem.headline: Supreme Court reverses lower court in property case.

text.p: The Supreme Court Tuesday said a landowner could sue the local planning agency to get clearance to develop her land even though she had not tried a recourse the agency had offered to build elsewhere.

In a case closely watched by property rights advocates, the high court struck down a lower court ruling that threw out a lawsuit brought by an elderly woman against the California-Nevada Lake Tahoe Regional Planning Agency.

The lower court said she could not sue because she had not first tried to market "transferable development rights" (TRDs), which are variances from the planning and zoning regulations that can be sold or traded.

The case stemmed from Bernadine Suitum's effort to build a small house on property she owned near Lake Tahoe in Nevada. The planning commission said the land was near a stream and could not be developed.
Suitum sued the agency in 1991, saying its decision to bar construction of a house on the land was an unconstitutional taking of her property.

The lower court sided with the planning agency, which said the lawsuit was premature because Suitum had not tried to use her TRDs. However, Suitum said the TDR program was a "sham," and the transferable rights were of little or no value.
The majority of the high court said TDR's should be factored into a decision on whether there was a property taking, but said the landowner cannot be required to try to market them.

"Governments should not be allowed to concoct elaborate schemes that deprive property owners of their right to just compensation," Nancie Marzulla, chief counsel for Defenders of Property Rights, said in a statement.
The Environmental Defense Fund, which has pushed TDRs as an economical way to avoid development on sensitive land, said the Supreme Court ruling did not undermine TDR programs.

"The Supreme Court has left undisturbed its precedent that tradeable development rights must be considered when deciding whether government must pay landowners to enforce local land use rules," EDF senior attorney Tim Searchinger said.
